> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

$(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets there is a sequence
$(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ with $a_n\in A_n$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Thus the

$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Expressing each column of $X$ in this basis gives $X=QR$, where $R$ is upper triangular; its diagonal entries are the nonzero Gram–Schmidt residual norms, so $R$ is invertible. By [F3], extend the columns of $Q$ to an orthonormal basis $[Q\ Q_0]$ of $\mathbb R^n$.

Set $U=[Q\ Q_0]$. Then $U$ is orthogonal. Standardizing the independent errors gives $\eta=\varepsilon/\sigma$ with independent standard-normal coordinates, so [F4] makes $U^T\eta=(Z_Q,Z_0)$ a standard-normal product vector with independent coordinate blocks. Since $X=QR$ and $X^TX=R^TR$, the normal-equation solution in [F1] is $\widehat\beta=R^{-1}Q^TY=\beta+\sigma R^{-1}Z_Q$. Substituting $X=QR$ and $(R^TR)^{-1}=R^{-1}R^{-T}$ gives $P_X=Q R(R^TR)^{-1}R^TQ^T=Q[RR^{-1}R^{-T}R^T]Q^T=QQ^T$, because $RR^{-1}=I_p$ and $R^{-T}R^T=I_p$. Since $U$ is orthogonal, $I_n-P_X=Q_0Q_0^T$. Thus $(I_n-P_X)Y=\sigma Q_0Z_0$, so $RSS_X/\sigma^2=\|Z_0\|^2\sim\chi_{n-p}^2$ by [F5]. By [A2] and [F7], the linear maps defining $\widehat\beta$ and $Q_0Z_0$, and the squared-norm map defining $RSS_X$, are Borel; hence these quantities are measurable functions of the independent coordinate blocks and $\widehat\beta$ is independent of $RSS_X$ by [F4]. The map defining $\widehat\beta$ is linear and Borel, so it is a statistic for the stated experiment. The residual map and squared norm are continuous, so $RSS_X$ and $S$ are continuous. The piecewise t version in the Statement is Borel: its quotient is continuous on the Borel set $S>0$ and its value on $S=0$ is constant. Its denominator has positive degree $n-p$, hence $S>0$ almost surely by [F5].

For $c\ne0$, put $v=R^{-T}c$. Invertibility of $R$ gives $v\ne0$. Complete $v/\|v\|$ to an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb R^p$ by [F3]; applying [F4] to the resulting orthogonal matrix shows $G_c=v^TZ_Q/\|v\|\sim N(0,1)$. Under [A2], the continuous linear map defining $G_c$ is Borel. It is independent of $Q_0:=\|Z_0\|^2\sim\chi_{n-p}^2$, because $Z_Q$ and $Z_0$ are independent blocks and $G_c$ and the squared-norm map are measurable functions of those blocks. Since $X^TX=R^TR$, $\|v\|^2=c^TR^{-1}R^{-T}c=c^T(X^TX)^{-1}c$. Thus on $Q_0>0$ the displayed contrast ratio is $G_c/\sqrt{Q_0/(n-p)}$; on $Q_0=0$ its version $\widetilde T_c$ is zero. This is exactly the extension in the definition of $t_{n-p}$, so [F5]–[F6] give $\widetilde T_c\sim t_{n-p}$.

For the nested models, let $W_D=W_U\cap W_R^\perp$. The finite-dimensional orthogonal decompositions in [F3] give $\mathbb R^n=W_R\oplus W_D\oplus W_U^\perp$, with dimensions $p-q,q,n-p$. Choose orthonormal bases in these three spaces and concatenate them into an orthogonal matrix $V$. By [F4], the coordinates of $V^T\varepsilon/\sigma$ in the three blocks are independent standard normals. Under the null, $P_R(X\beta)=P_U(X\beta)=X\beta$, so $(I-P_R)Y=(I-P_R)\varepsilon=P_{W_D}\varepsilon+P_{W_U^\perp}\varepsilon$ and $(I-P_U)Y=(I-P_U)\varepsilon=P_{W_U^\perp}\varepsilon$: here [F8] identifies $I-P_R=P_{W_R^\perp}$ and $I-P_U=P_{W_U^\perp}$, while the direct sum in [F3] splits the first projection into the two orthogonal components. The coordinate-block maps and the linear projections are continuous, and squared norms are continuous, so [A2] and [F7] make all these random vectors and real variables measurable. Orthogonality and [F9] give $RSS_R-RSS_U=\sigma^2\sum_{j=1}^{q}G_j^2$ and $RSS_U=\sigma^2\sum_{j=1}^{n-p}H_j^2$, where the $G$ and $H$ coordinate blocks are independent standard-normal blocks. By [F5] these sums are independent $\sigma^2\chi_q^2$ and $\sigma^2\chi_{n-p}^2$ variables; both degrees are positive. The piecewise ratio $\widetilde F$ is Borel, since it is continuous on the Borel set $RSS_U>0$ and constant on $RSS_U=0$. Its value is the scaled ratio on $Q_H:=\sum_{j=1}^{n-p}H_j^2>0$ and $0$ when $Q_H=0$; by [F6] this is exactly the defined $F_{q,n-p}$ version. The F denominator is positive almost surely by [F5], so $\widetilde F\sim F_{q,n-p}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. For every sequence
$(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets there is a sequence
$(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ with $a_n\in A_n$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Thus the
Axiom of Choice implies the pair-local countable choice principle
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z\sim N_n(0,I_n)$, and let $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be an orthogonal projection of rank $r$, where $0\le r\le n$. Then the random vectors $PZ$ and $(I_n-P)Z$ are independent, and
$$
\|PZ\|^2\sim\chi_r^2,\qquad \|(I_n-P)Z\|^2\sim\chi_{n-r}^2.
$$
The two squared norms are independent. The cases $r=0$ and $r=n$ are included, with $\chi_0^2=\delta_0$.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every integer $k\ge1$, the law $\chi_k^2$ has density
$$
f_k(x)=c_k x^{k/2-1}e^{-x/2}\mathbf 1_{\{x>0\}},\qquad c_k=\frac{\sigma_{k-1}(S^{k-1})}{2(2\pi)^{k/2}}>0,
$$
where $\sigma_{k-1}$ is the polar surface measure on the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^k$. Consequently, $Q_k>0$ almost surely, and its cumulative distribution function is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a positive integer $k$, take the product probability law of an independent standard normal $G$ and an independent $Q_k\sim\chi_k^2$. The **Student t law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $t_k$, is the law of
$$
T_k=\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{G}{\sqrt{Q_k/k}},&Q_k>0,\\
0,&Q_k=0.
\end{cases}
$$
For positive integers $r,s$, take independent $Q_r\sim\chi_r^2$ and $Q_s\sim\chi_s^2$. The **Fisher F law with degrees $(r,s)$**, denoted $F_{r,s}$, is the law of
$$
F_{r,s}=\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{Q_r/r}{Q_s/s},&Q_s>0,\\
0,&Q_s=0.
\end{cases}
$$
The displayed piecewise maps are Borel measurable: each quotient is continuous on its Borel positive-denominator region, and the value on the Borel zero set is constant. The positive-degree chi-square lemma proves that the denominators are positive almost surely, so these versions agree almost surely with the usual quotients. Zero degrees are excluded from both definitions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every $k\ge1$, the CDF of $t_k$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, is symmetric about zero, and has limits $0$ and $1$ at $-\infty$ and $+\infty$. For every $r,s\ge1$, the CDF of $F_{r,s}$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$, is zero on $(-\infty,0]$, and is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$ with limit $1$ at $+\infty$. Consequently, for each $u\in(0,1)$ each law has exactly one $u$-quantile on its support.

derivations.claim: By [A2], Countable Choice holds, so [F2] applies to the linear continuous map $x\mapsto\bar x$; hence it is a statistic on the stated Borel data space. Put $Z_i=(X_i-\mu)/\sigma$. The affine pushforward definition in [F1] gives each $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$, and [F1] preserves their independence. Thus $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\sim N_n(0,I_n)$ by [F4].

Define $\bar Z=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i$, $u=n^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1)^T$, and $P=uu^T$. Since $u^Tu=1$, $P$ is a rank-one orthogonal projection. We have $u^TZ=\sqrt n\,\bar Z$ and $X-\bar X(1,\ldots,1)^T=\sigma(I_n-P)Z$. Therefore $\bar X=\mu+\sigma u^TZ/\sqrt n$ and $S^2=\sigma^2\|(I_n-P)Z\|^2/(n-1)$.

By [F3], $PZ$ and $(I_n-P)Z$ are independent and $Q:=\|(I_n-P)Z\|^2\sim\chi_{n-1}^2$. The continuous linear map $z\mapsto u^Tz$ is Borel by [A2] and [F2], and $u^TZ=u^TPZ$; the continuous squared-norm map on the complementary vector is likewise Borel. Thus $G:=u^TZ$ and $Q$ are measurable functions of the independent vectors in [F3], so they are independent by [F1]. By [F4], $G\sim N(0,1)$.

The formulas in step 1.2 express $\bar X$ as an affine function of $G$ and $S^2$ as $\sigma^2 Q/(n-1)$. Hence $\bar X$ and $S^2$ are independent, $(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2=Q\sim\chi_{n-1}^2$, and $S>0$ almost surely by [F5].

The set $\{S>0\}$ is Borel and the displayed quotient is continuous there; assigning $0$ on $\{S=0\}$ therefore makes $\widetilde T$ measurable. Since $S=0$ exactly when $Q=0$, step 1.2 gives $\widetilde T=G/\sqrt{Q/(n-1)}$ on $\{Q>0\}$ and both versions are $0$ on $\{Q=0\}$. The variables $G$ and $Q$ are independent with laws $N(0,1)$ and $\chi_{n-1}^2$, so [F5] gives $\widetilde T\sim t_{n-1}$.

Let $q=q_{n-1}(1-\alpha/2)$. By [F5], the $t_{n-1}$ CDF is continuous and symmetric, so $F_{t_{n-1}}(0)=1/2<1-\alpha/2$ and strict increase gives $q>0$; symmetry then gives $F_{t_{n-1}}(-q)=\alpha/2$. Step 3.1 therefore gives $\mathbb P(-q\le\widetilde T\le q)=1-\alpha$. On the full-probability event $\{S>0\}$ from step 2.2, this event is exactly $\{\mu\text{ lies in the displayed interval}\}$ by multiplying by $S/\sqrt n$ and rearranging. The events agree almost surely, so the interval has exact coverage $1-\alpha$.
